newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader agrees to meet Mobutu on ship.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader agrees to meet Mobutu on ship.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Tuesday he had agreed to meet President Mobutu Sese Seko on a ship in the Atlantic to discuss a transfer of power in Kinshasa.
Kabila announced his agreement to a meeting shortly after his rebels entered the town of Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from Kinshasa, and were greeted by crowds of jubilant residents.

Shortly before the announcement, U.S. troubleshooter Bill Richardson met Mobutu in Kinshasa and told reporters that the president and Kabila should meet face-to-face immediately. Richardson was expected to meet Kabila later on Tuesday.

"I have agreed to (South African) President (Nelson) Mandela's request that I meet Mr Mobutu on a ship off the Atlantic coastline to discuss Mr Mobutu's departure," Kabila told Reuters, adding the ship would be a South African navy vessel off the coast of Zaire.
"As far as I am concerned this will be a short ceremony at which Mr Mobutu is supposed to agree to leave, otherwise our forces now advancing on the route to Kinshasa will eject him.
"I am made to believe he (Mobutu) will cooprate with us and avoid a bloody confrontation for Kinshasa," Kabila added.
He said talks would go hand-in-hand with a rebel offensive and said rebels were advancing towards Kinshasa from Kikwit.

Asked about the date for their first face-to-face meeting, he said it would be in the next few days and Mandela and U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun were working on an agreeable date but the most important thing was that both sides had agreed to meet.

Before leaving Kinshasa for Lubumbashi, Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said: "We are after a date. Perhaps we will know more this afternoon. The sooner the better, perhaps this weekend would be an important goal."

In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said it had "increasingly shocking reports" of killings of refugees around Kisangani and other areas of eastern Zaire held by the rebels and demanded a full investigation.
Richardson met Mobutu for 90 minutes at his presidential villa inside Kinshasa's heavily defended Camp Tshatshi by the Zaire River and gave him a letter from President Bill Clinton.
"My meeting with President Mobutu was a good one. We were both very frank. I carried a strong message but at the same time I think we made progress," he said.
South Africa said earlier on Tuesday talks between the two civil war foes, chaired by Mandela, were imminent.

"The talks will take place shortly...it will be a meeting between President Mobutu and Laurent Kabila," a spokesman for its Department of Foreign Affairs said in Johannesburg. The venue was not given.
Mobutu, who has cancer, has ruled out South Africa as too far on health grounds. Kabila has ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, and Gabon on security grounds.
South Africa's Business Day newspaper said the South African naval supply ship Outeniqua could host the talks in international waters off Zaire or Angola's neighbouring Cabinda enclave.

A senior rebel commander said in Lubumbashi that Mobutu's Presidential Guard strongly defended Kikwit airport, which rebels needed as a springboard for a final assault on Kinshasa. But Kabila later said his men had seized the airport as well.
Richardson also plans to visit Zaire's rebel-held third city of Kisangani and possibly Angola, which Kinshasa has accused of invading Zaire to back the rebels.

Diplomatic sources said there was concern that Angola, struggling to establish its own fragile peace process, could be sucked into the Zaire war with government forces backing the rebels and former UNITA rebels backing the Zairean government.
The rebels, fighting since October, control over half of Zaire, Africa's third largest nation at the continent's heart.
Richardson's trip to Kisangani will focus on the plight of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans.
The rebels have been accused of driving the Hutu refugees into the jungle in the hope that they will die there. Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days to repatriate them to Rwanda.

"We are receiving increasingly shocking reports of killings of refugees both in the area around Kisangani and elsewhere," Pamela O'Toole, U.N. refugee agency spokeswoman. "These killings must stop and an urgent investigation must be launched."
